generatedProse.concept-context: Across any field of study, success is tempting to read straight off a transcript. Yet a degree develops you in ways a grade never shows: the independence to work on your own, the care to weigh evidence, the resilience to act on hard feedback. Defining success on your own terms means naming both the performance and this personal development. As you become a graduate, being able to articulate that development, with evidence from projects and placements, is what employers and further study ask for.
generatedProse.worked-example:
Consider two students asked, at a graduation event, what their degree gave them.

{{learner-a}} answers with the classification alone: a good grade, and relief that it is over. It is an honest account of academic performance, but it stops there. {{learner-a}} has not defined success in any personal way, so there is nothing to say about who they have become, and the development that did happen goes unclaimed.

{{learner-b}} answers with both kinds. The grade is there, but so is a clear account: I set out to become someone who could work independently and handle hard feedback, and here is the project and the placement that show I can. That is success defined on their own terms and backed with evidence.

Both graduated. Only {{learner-b}} had defined what success meant and could articulate the development to prove it.
generatedProse.summary: Success comes in two kinds: academic performance, your results, and personal development, who you become through the work. Defining success on your own terms means setting a good outcome across both, rather than inheriting a single measure. As you become a graduate, the decisive skill is articulation: saying, with evidence from your projects and placements, what you set out to do and what you can now do.

check.body: In the worked example, what did {{learner-b}} do that {{learner-a}} did not?

items.text: Defined success on their own terms, across both performance and personal development.
Avoided any setbacks during the degree.

feedback.correct: That's right. {{learner-b}} defined success on their own terms, across both kinds, and could evidence it.
feedback.incorrectNotFinal: Not quite. Look for what {{learner-b}} could say about success, not how they scored or how fast they finished.
feedback.incorrectFinal: {{learner-b}} defined success on their own terms across both kinds. A higher grade, greater speed or avoided setbacks are not what the example turns on.

_prompts.concept-context: What does this look like in practice within the given context? Write a short follow-on from the generic definition above, in the learner's own subject or discipline. Keep it to two or three sentences, mid-register, following straight on from the generic definition.
_prompts.worked-example: Give a subject-specific worked example of this lesson's concept: a weaker or less-developed version first, then a stronger version reached by better practice, using the context cast (character tokens) consistently. Keep the weaker-then-stronger shape and the two-part contrast; carry the cast only through the {{learner-a}} (weaker) and {{learner-b}} (stronger) tokens, never a literal name (the pack supplies the whole body, but not the names). Each example paragraph must begin with its token, weaker first - merge-context.js's wrapProse() only emits the we-weaker/we-stronger cue classes for a paragraph that leads with the token. The merge renders it as a block quote, so write it as continuous prose, not as a quoted comment plus commentary.
_prompts.summary: Recap what the learner can now do, in terms of their own subject or context. One short paragraph. Do not restate the learning outcomes verbatim.
_prompts.check: Write the subject's own version of this lesson's check question(s), testing the same outcome in the learner's own discipline. Keep the same number of items and the same correctness pattern as the generic version; reword the stem and items for the subject. Keep the component-level feedback (correct / notFinal / final) teaching, never a bare verdict.
